overview: This bill expands the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, a 1995 law meant to make federal agencies consider the costs their rules place on state, local and tribal governments and private businesses. For any "major rule" (one expected to have at least a $100 million yearly effect on the economy or other significant impacts), agencies would have to publish detailed cost-benefit studies, compare alternatives, and generally choose the option with the greatest net benefits unless the White House regulatory review office approves otherwise. It also requires earlier consultation with state and local officials and affected businesses, advance public notice before major rules are proposed, and annual compliance reports to Congress. The bill extends these requirements to independent agencies (except for the Federal Reserve's monetary policy) and lets people harmed by a rule sue over whether the agency followed the new analysis rules. As of January 13, 2026, a House committee had approved an amended version and it was placed on the House calendar for a vote.
for: Supporters say agencies should carefully weigh costs to governments, businesses and workers before issuing expensive rules, and that more analysis and consultation will lead to smarter, more transparent regulations.
against: Critics say the added studies, review steps and new grounds for lawsuits would slow down or block rules that protect health, safety and the environment, and give a White House office more control over independent agencies.
